shows.title: Nymphäum
shows.description:
Anselm Kiefer turns the vast industrial halls of Thaddaeus Ropac's Pantin outpost into a painterly sanctuary dedicated to nymphs, the minor deities of springs, rivers and groves in classical mythology. Across more than twenty new paintings, some spanning many meters of canvas, he layers lead, straw, gold leaf, shellac and the jade-toned residue of electrolysis into surfaces so thick they read almost as topography. Bathing figures dissolve into dark water, faces emerge camouflaged among foliage, and in the exhibition's most staggering work, a nearly eight-meter-wide vision of mountain nymphs, Kiefer reworks a nineteenth-century academic painting into something bleaker and more geological.

What makes the show compelling isn't just its scale, which is considerable even by Kiefer's own monumental standards, but the way it braids together two of his oldest preoccupations: the classical past as a wound that keeps reopening, and the natural world's slow reconquest of ruined, man-made terrain. Some canvases replace his familiar scorched landscapes with glowing city grids inspired by light through the trees of Central Park, their windows built from meticulous gold leaf, while vines and collaged straw seem to physically pierce through from behind, as if nature were clawing back the frame itself.

Kiefer has spent more than five decades turning myth, alchemy and the trauma of European history into material fact, and Nymphäum feels like a late, ambitious chapter in that project. It's a demanding show, dense with reference and sheer physical weight, but it rewards close looking: the closer you get to these surfaces, the more they seem to move.

shows.title: TILL DEATH DO US PART
shows.description:
Sterling Ruby turns the rue de Castiglione space into an elegy for the cut flower. Cast bronze sculptures from his ongoing "Bound Flowers. Couple." series pair up blooms in embracing, wedding-portrait poses — stiff, formal, a little morbid — while large cyanotype-based collages from the "GHOSTS" series paper the walls in dense blue fields drawn from his garden in Vernon, California and time spent in the Eastern Sierras.

The show leans hard on the vanitas tradition, nodding to seventeenth-century Dutch and Flemish still life painting where cut flowers stood in for beauty's expiration date. Ruby's bronzes literalize that decay: petals frozen mid-wilt, stems bound together in poses that read as much like restraint as affection. It's a tighter, more focused presentation than some of his sprawling installations, built around a single material metaphor — the "till death do us part" of the title — worked through in two very different registers, sculptural and photographic.

Worth seeing for anyone tracking how an artist known for maximalist scale and industrial materials handles something as fragile and traditional as a flower painting, and for the bronzes alone, which are genuinely strange objects up close.

shows.title: Annette Messager: Histoires des oreillers
shows.description:
This "In Focus" presentation is a concentrated look at Annette Messager's decades-long habit of turning soft, domestic materials — pillows, embroidery, tulle veils, netting, a broom — into vehicles for wordplay, intimacy and quiet subversion. The anchor piece, Histoire des oreillers III (1995–2026), hangs rows of pillows on black cord, some fitted with small framed photographs of body fragments, so that an ordinary object charged with sleep and the body becomes a kind of confessional archive.

Around it the gallery has assembled pieces spanning fifty years: Les Qualificatifs données aux femmes (1972), an early, quietly furious embroidery of misogynist epithets in colored thread on black cloth; Les Lignes de la main (1988), photographs of open palms overlaid with obsessively repeated handwritten words; and Just Married (2011), a broom draped in a bridal veil that turns a marriage ritual into something closer to a ghost story. Spleen (2025), a sagging wire-and-netting word-sculpture, is having its public debut here.

Messager, who won the Golden Lion representing France at the 2005 Venice Biennale, is having a substantial Paris moment: this show runs alongside her larger survey at the Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature nearby, and the gallery presentation deliberately picks up threads — romantic imagery, secrecy, sexual politics — that the museum show doesn't foreground. Seeing rarely-shown historic pieces like these in a relatively intimate gallery setting is the real draw for anyone who knows her mainly through the big installations.

shows.title: Ciphering African Acacias and Supreme Court Decisions
shows.description:
Charles Gaines has spent fifty years building systems — rule-based, self-determined procedures that generate artworks whose outcomes even he can't fully predict. This first Paris show pairs two bodies of work that show that method operating on very different kinds of material: nature and law.

The Plexiglas grid works extend his long-running Numbers and Trees series, begun in 1986, into new territory: acacias photographed on a 2023 trip to Tanzania, each tree assigned a color and broken into cells, then layered so individual identities survive the overlay rather than dissolving into it. Gaines names each tree after a local tribal group, folding histories of colonialism and displacement into what looks, at a glance, like pure abstraction. The companion piece, Manifestos 7, takes a harder political turn: Gaines translates the language of two landmark US Supreme Court rulings — Plessy v. Ferguson and Brown v. Board of Education — into musical notation, producing an audiovisual installation where legal text becomes an unsettling, semi-random score.

It's a rigorous, quietly devastating pairing — one work about the arbitrary categories we impose on nature, the other about the arbitrary and violent categories the law has imposed on people — and a good introduction to why Gaines is considered a bridge between 1970s conceptualism and the identity-driven conceptual art that followed him.

shows.title: Hauser and Wirth Invite(s): Arthur Gillet
shows.description:
Painted on sheets of copper, this small show is the sixth Paris edition of Hauser and Wirth's ongoing initiative to host outside artists, galleries and writers on the second floor of its own space. Arthur Gillet made the work inside Enver Hoxha's former villa in Tirana, using copper both for its material history — soft enough to engrave, conductive enough to have carried voices and images across Albania's Cold War-era surveillance networks — and for its personal resonance with the artist's own biography.

Gillet grew up with deaf parents in a family shaped as much by invention as by silence, and the show threads that experience through Albania's recent history: the improvised radio receivers Albanians built to catch forbidden broadcasts, the hidden microphones of the Sigurimi, and testimony from Shpetim Zero, a survivor of a forced labor camp whose voice enters the installation through an old Albanian radio. The connective tissue is communication itself — who gets heard, who gets surveilled, and what happens when the same technology carries both.

It's a dense, research-driven project for a "guest exhibition" slot, produced with La collective Greater Paris and accompanied by a text from art historian Patricia Falguières, and worth seeing as much for the unusual copper-as-canvas technique as for the political history embedded in it.

shows.title: Pays rêvé, pays réel
shows.artist: Merikokeb Berhanu, Sanford Biggers, Julien Creuzet, Jamal Cyrus, Leslie Hewitt, Jason Moran, Thomias Radin
shows.description:
Curator Lucien Terras borrows his title from Édouard Glissant's 1985 poetry collection, using the Martinican writer's thinking on relation, creolization and diasporic identity as the framework for this group show. Painting, sculpture, sound and video by a transatlantic roster of artists trace the distance between an imagined homeland and a lived one, moving between Africa, the Caribbean, the American South and Europe without settling into any single narrative of origin.

The Paris presentation is the second half of a two-venue project that began jointly with Galerie Natalie Seroussi; this iteration brings together Berhanu's dense botanical abstractions, Biggers's quilt-based cosmologies, Creuzet's diasporic assemblages, the collaborative textile-and-sound works of Jamal Cyrus and Leslie Hewitt, and musician-artist Jason Moran's scores-as-objects alongside Thomias Radin's material investigations. The result reads less like a survey than a constellation, each artist offering a different register — historical, poetic, sonic — for thinking about migration and belonging.

It's a smart, tightly argued show for a gallery known for conceptually rigorous programming, and a rare chance to see Glissant's ideas made concrete through contemporary practice rather than treated as academic reference.

shows.title: Entresueños
shows.description:
Mercedes Llanos's second solo show at Balice Hertling is built around a recurring motif: the bed, rendered as an oversized, almost architectural presence across several large oil paintings (some stretching over four meters). Titled "Entresueños" — literally "between dreams" — the works sit in the woozy space between sleep and waking, using graphite alongside oil to draw out spirals, stains, and half-formed marks that read as much like psychological residue as depicted objects.

Llanos, an Argentine painter based in New York, pairs these bed paintings with smaller still lifes — dried flowers, wilting arrangements, objects on the verge of decay — that push the same mood of suspended, private time into a quieter register. The palette runs from radioactive reds to bruised umbers, and the scale swings from intimate wood-panel paintings to canvases large enough to dwarf a viewer, giving the show a rhythm of intimacy and overwhelm.

For anyone who caught Llanos's first Paris show in 2022, this is a clear continuation of her interest in the bedroom as a site of both comfort and unease — worth a visit before it closes.

shows.title: Rat-A-Hum-Tat-Tat-Rat-A-Hum-Tat-Tat
shows.description:
For his first show with the gallery, Xiao Guo Hui fills the street-facing window of Pièce Unique — MASSIMODECARLO's single-work project space in the Marais — with one large diptych, over two meters wide, about noise. Painted in egg tempera and fresco rather than oil, using techniques the artist learned from Cennino Cennini's Renaissance-era handbook, the picture splits into two scenes: on one side the mechanized racket of street cleaners, leaf blowers and construction equipment that plagued the eight years Xiao and his wife lived in the Marais; on the other, a crowd of dancers in a fictionalized version of Place Colette, absorbed in noise of their own choosing.

Xiao trained in oil painting in Guangzhou before abandoning it for the slower, hand-ground materials of pre-Renaissance panel painting, and that choice of technique is part of the work's argument — a refusal of the smooth, "suffocating" finish he associates with the city's own compulsion toward cleanliness and order. His wife, the designer and painter Chen Wen Qing, makes the costumes for every painted figure, giving each dancer a specific, legible identity the way a quattrocento portrait does.

Because the gallery's window opens directly onto the street, the painting is meant to be read against the real noise and traffic passing in front of it — a deliberately small, pointed gesture rather than a survey show, on view for just under two weeks.

shows.title: Petits Formats
shows.description:
Small-scale works are the organizing conceit of this group presentation at Skarstedt's Paris outpost, which strings together a century of modern and contemporary art through the intimacy of the miniature. The checklist ranges wide: Basquiat and Warhol alongside Bonnard, Boudin and Vuillard, Picasso and Dubuffet next to Cindy Sherman and Yves Klein, with sculptors like John Chamberlain and Hans Josephsohn also working in reduced scale.

The pleasure of a show like this is the whiplash of putting a nineteenth-century Boudin seascape a few feet from a Warhol or a Sherman film still — pieces that share nothing stylistically but everything in terms of scale and the demand they make for close, quiet looking rather than the sweeping glance a large canvas invites. It's less an argument about a movement or a moment than a connoisseur's cabinet, built to let the gallery's inventory of blue-chip names talk to each other in an unusually informal register.

For visitors who know these artists mainly from museum-scale masterworks, seeing them shrunk down to petit format offers a different kind of encounter — more like leafing through a private collection than touring a survey. It's a summer-season show in the loosest sense, worth a stop for the sheer density of well-known hands packed into a single room.

shows.title: Lucio Fontana: Ceramics
shows.dates_note: Gallery page marks the show "Prolonged, through 5 September 2026" (its final day)
shows.description:
This is a rare chance to see Lucio Fontana away from the slashed canvases he's best known for. The show gathers ceramic works spanning the 1930s through the 1960s, tracing a medium Fontana returned to throughout his career, one rooted in his childhood in his father's monumental-sculpture workshop. It opens with the 1938 Torso Italico, a fragmented, armless figure that nods to antique sculpture while quietly undercutting the monumental classicism of its moment.

From there the exhibition moves through very different registers: the loose, brightly colored menagerie of animals and shells Fontana made in Albisola with the ceramicist Tullio Mazzotti, wartime-inflected battle scenes and crucifixion imagery worked with real gestural violence, and finally the large, pierced Natura terracottas of the late 1950s, whose gouged and perforated surfaces translate his spatialist ideas about surface and void into clay rather than canvas.

Seen together, the works make the case that ceramics were not a sideline for Fontana but a parallel laboratory where his ideas about breaking through the picture plane first took physical form. For a gallery that has represented the artist since 1973, this is a chance to make an argument for the ceramics as central rather than peripheral to his project, and the installation photographs show a tightly hung, object-dense presentation that rewards close looking at surface and texture.

shows.title: Tendrement
shows.description:
Mathieu Cherkit paints the house he lives in and the garden around it, over and over, in a thick, physical impasto that turns domestic subject matter — doorways, staircases, houseplants, a kitchen table — into something closer to landscape painting than interior scene. Tendrement (Tenderly) is the latest chapter in that long-running project, painted with the same loaded brush and high-key palette that has become his signature.

There's a deliberate lack of drama in Cherkit's choice of subjects: a windowsill, a patch of garden, the corner of a room caught in afternoon light. What carries the work is the paint handling itself — thick, almost sculptural strokes built up wet-on-wet, so that ordinary domestic space starts to feel charged and unstable, on the edge of abstraction even as the subject stays perfectly legible.

The title suggests an unusually gentle register for an artist whose paintings can otherwise feel almost aggressive in their materiality, and the show reads as a warm, close-focus survey of the rooms and corners Cherkit knows best.

shows.title: Jason Dodge
shows.description:
Jason Dodge's work has long operated by quiet substitution: an everyday material or found object is renamed, re-routed, or paired with a spare, often poetic title, and the resulting sculpture asks viewers to slow down and reconstruct the chain of decisions behind it. This new exhibition at Galerie Allen continues that practice, following recent solo presentations at Kunsthalle Friart Fribourg and a collaborative show earlier at Mudam Luxembourg.

Dodge, an American sculptor based on the Danish island of Møn, works with things like thread, metal, glass, and light — materials that carry traces of labor and place without announcing themselves as spectacular. His installations tend to be understated in the room and considerable in the mind afterward; a spool of thread dyed by hand, a length of pipe, an arrangement of found or fabricated objects, each accompanied by wall text that functions almost like a short poem.

This is Dodge's second solo outing with the gallery, and it arrives at a moment of wide institutional attention for the artist, with parallel exhibitions on view this year in Switzerland and Poland. Visitors should expect a spare, deliberate installation that rewards unhurried looking over quick consumption.

shows.title: This Is Where We Are (Nous en sommes là)
shows.description:
Joseph Grigely, an artist and writer who has been deaf since childhood, was invited by the Palais de Tokyo to take over one of the building's least accessible corners — and instead of smoothing it over, he makes the friction the entire subject. The piece confronts visitors with the museum's own architectural failures: stairs with no ramp, routes that quietly exclude anyone using a wheelchair, thresholds that assume a body that moves a certain way.

Grigely is best known for his "Conversation Pieces," works built from the scraps of paper hearing people have used to talk to him over the years — notes that become fragmented scripts of misheard, half-finished, or hastily written exchanges. That practice of assembling meaning out of broken communication carries over here: cracked and reassembled sculptural heads, damaged walls, and a risograph publication all speak to the idea of an "access prosthesis," his term for the makeshift tools and workarounds disabled people build for themselves when institutions don't.

Rather than proposing a tidy fix, the exhibition treats accessibility as an unresolved, structural problem — one baked into the history of how cultural buildings get designed and who they're designed for. It's a quieter, more conceptual entry in the Palais de Tokyo's current season than some of its neighbors, but it rewards visitors willing to read the wall texts and the debris as carefully as they'd read a painting.

shows.title: Les Ambassadeurs
shows.description:
Jesse Darling, who won the Turner Prize in 2023, fills the Palais de Tokyo's great glass-roofed nave with a fleet of tattered flags, worn lecterns and industrial fans that keep the fabric fluttering in an endless, slightly pathetic ceremony. The installation borrows its title from Holbein's 1533 double portrait "The Ambassadors," a painting famous for its warped skull hidden in plain sight, and Darling uses that same trick of distortion to talk about power that has curdled and lost its nerve.

The work is built from the artist's usual vocabulary: scavenged materials, cheap industrial hardware, bandaged and patched surfaces that look like they've survived some kind of accident. Podiums stand empty or nearly so, banners have gone illegible, and the whole tableau reads like the diplomatic corps of a government nobody quite remembers electing. It's a show about entropy and the slow-motion collapse of institutional authority, staged with a wit that keeps it from tipping into didacticism.

Darling has spoken about wanting to register the fragility of the systems around us — economic, political, physical — without falling into either despair or easy cynicism, and that ambivalence gives the piece its charge. Site-specific and built especially for this cavernous room, it's one of the more ambitious single-artist takeovers the Palais de Tokyo has staged this season, and worth seeing simply for the sculptural theater of dozens of fans animating a graveyard of symbols.

shows.title: Moving Colors
shows.description:
This group exhibition treats color not as decoration but as the whole argument, tracing a line from Josef Albers's rigorously systematic "Homage to the Square" studies through the postwar Italian artists who took his logic and pushed it toward optical and kinetic extremes. Piero Dorazio's woven color fields, Carla Accardi's acid-toned marks on transparent sicofoil, Giorgio Griffa's unstretched canvases, and Alberto Biasi's retina-teasing "oggetti ottico-dinamici" all treat hue as a physical and perceptual event rather than a descriptive tool.

The show's real coup is pulling Alighiero Boetti's embroidered "Tutto" into this conversation — a mosaic of interlocking silhouettes stitched by Afghan craftswomen under a rule that no two adjacent shapes could share a color, turning painterly color theory into a textile logic problem. Lee Sung-Kuen's threaded sculptures pick up that same idea of color given physical body decades later, while Dadamaino's "Ricerca del colore" series and Victor Vasarely's Op Art anchor the show's more clinical, perception-testing wing.

Given Tornabuoni's specialty in twentieth-century Italian art, this is very much a gallery's-eye survey rather than a museum thesis show — a chance to see Arte Povera-adjacent and Op Art names in dialogue with Albers and Vasarely without the didactic scaffolding of an institutional wall text. It rewards visitors who like to look slowly and let the optical effects do the talking.

shows.title: Mes années 80
shows.description:
Gallerist Claudine Papillon turns the summer show over to her own memory, pulling together a group exhibition built around the artists and decades that have shaped the gallery's identity since it opened in the 1980s. Rather than a themed curatorial premise, "Mes années 80" (My 1980s) reads as a personal cross-section: sculpture, watercolor, photography and mixed-media work by a long roster of gallery artists including Elsa Sahal, Sabrina Vitali, Gaëlle Chotard, Céline Cléron, Javier Pérez, Günter Brus, Dieter Roth and Erik Dietman, spanning generations and mediums rather than a single visual argument.

Sahal's glazed ceramic bodies and Vitali's raw, visceral sculptural fragments sit at very different ends of the gallery's program from historic figures like Dieter Roth or the Viennese Actionist Günter Brus, and that range is the point: this is a portrait of a program built through accumulation and long-term relationships with artists rather than trend-chasing.

It's a loose, affectionate survey rather than a tightly argued thesis show, best approached as a walk through one dealer's history of looking, a chance to see how disparate practices, brought together under one roof over four decades, still make sense as a single, coherent sensibility.

shows.title: Vallée FM
shows.description:
Pierre Bellot's new paintings drop the pretense of subject matter altogether: no still life, no landscape to anchor the eye, just surface, color, and the friction of tones worked against each other. The pictures start from instinct — a fast, chaotic first pass — and build slowly from there, sometimes over years, with older canvases scraped back and repainted until earlier layers show through as pentimenti, small geological records of a picture changing its mind.

What emerges reads like a loose atlas: fragments that could be coastlines, city blocks, unfinished maps, or torn-off pieces of wall, each one eventually finding a title only after the image has already declared itself. Bellot works matte and chalky rather than glossy, chasing accidents rather than eliminating them, and the paintings' modest scale (many well under a meter) rewards close, slow looking rather than a quick pass through the room.

This is Bellot's continuing engagement with abstraction as a physical, studio-bound practice rather than a style — worth seeing for anyone curious about how a French painter working today handles the old problem of what a non-representational canvas is actually "of."

shows.title: Pastoral Melody
shows.description:
Hugo Ruyant's paintings work by slight displacement rather than declaration: recognizable forms that start to waver the moment you look closely, symbols that surface almost imperceptibly rather than announcing themselves. Pastoral Melody takes on one of painting's oldest set-pieces, the shepherd and flock, and quietly dismantles its usual hierarchy.

The shepherd is simply gone. Without a leader to organize them, the sheep stop reading as an undifferentiated mass and become individuals, each rendered with enough particularity to function as a kind of portrait. It's a small formal move with a bigger implication, an image bank built around order and submission repurposed to ask what collective identity looks like once the organizing authority disappears. Alongside the pastoral works, canvases of star-filled skies push the same idea outward, imaginary constellations and maps that lead nowhere in particular, opening the earthbound scenes onto a more cosmic, undetermined scale.

Ruyant treats color as an active structuring force here rather than decoration, generating what the accompanying text calls a "mental light" that keeps the motifs from settling into straightforward description. It's a show that uses inherited pictorial language, the pastoral, the constellation map, only to strip it of its old certainties, leaving paintings that pose the question of how images still guide us once their founding narratives no longer hold.

shows.title: Summer Break
shows.description:
Emanuela Campoli's late-summer presentation is a low-key, off-season hang rather than a curated thematic show — the kind of quiet group installment galleries use to keep their space open through August while staff and artists are between projects. It runs concurrently with a parallel "Summer Break" hang at the gallery's Milan space, underlining that this is one program shared across both cities rather than two unrelated exhibitions.

The gallery, founded in 2003 (originally as Campoli Presti before its rebrand), represents a cross-generational roster of American, French, and German artists working across painting, sculpture, and interdisciplinary media, and a summer show like this one is typically where a program's range is most visible — smaller pieces, varied media, less argument than a solo show would make. Worth a stop for anyone passing through the Marais who wants a sense of the gallery's program before its main autumn season begins.

shows.title: Always Again
shows.description:
Emmanuel Béguinot's first solo show at Derouillon is built entirely from portraits, but not the composed, flattering kind — these are faces and figures pulled apart by accumulation, torn paper, stains, and interrupted line. Drawing is the engine here: charcoal, ink and bitumen paint pile up on found or already-marked sheets until the image seems to buckle under its own weight, spilling past the edges of the frame or fragmenting into masks and loose studies pinned up alongside the finished works.

The frames themselves are part of the proposition. Béguinot builds them from plaster, foam, MDF, mirror, leather and wood, leaving hooks and joints exposed rather than concealed — a way of turning the domestic, respectable idea of the "family portrait" inside out. The result reads less like a series of discrete pictures than like a single unruly household of characters, caught somewhere between comedy and collapse.

There's a knowing, slightly feral humor running through the show, nodding to horror-film physiognomy and the exaggerated self-presentation of online "facemaxxing" culture as much as to older art-historical models of the grotesque. It's an uncomfortable, funny, and genuinely strange body of work, and a confident opening statement for an artist clearly not interested in tidy resolution.

shows.title: Intersections
shows.description:
Timed to the bicentennial of diplomatic relations between France and Mexico, this two-floor show pairs a French painter based in Mexico City with a Mexican painter working in the same city. It's a deliberate structure: the exhibition argues for cross-pollination between two art scenes without flattening what makes each artist's practice specific.

On the ground floor, Elsa-Louise Manceaux presents Surfaces of Exchange, built around a new radio-painting and a group of quieter, silent paintings that treat the canvas as a site where language, sound and moving image keep reshaping the composition. Upstairs, Hilda Palafox's Petricor continues her engagement with ecofeminism and collective labor: monumental female figures support and negotiate with one another until their bodies merge with the landscape — paintings named for the smell of earth after rain.

Together the two floors make a case for painting as a way of thinking about exchange itself — between bodies, languages, and two countries with two centuries of entangled history.

shows.title: Ernest Breleur
shows.description:
This is Ernest Breleur's first exhibition with Ceysson & Bénétière, bringing the Martinican artist's biomorphic abstractions to Paris. Breleur, a founding figure of the Martinican art movement Fwomajé, has spent decades developing a visual language rooted in Caribbean identity, memory, and the body, often working across painting, sculpture, and mixed media with materials like X-ray film, resin, and organic pigment.

The works on view are mostly untitled ("Sans titre"), dated across a wide span from 2010 to 2021, suggesting a mini-survey of the artist's recent decades of production rather than a single new body of work. Expect dense, layered surfaces where cellular and skeletal forms seem to float against dark or richly colored grounds — imagery that draws as much on biology and anatomy as on the folklore and political history of the French Caribbean.

For Paris audiences, this show is a rare chance to see an artist whose reputation has been built largely through Caribbean and francophone institutional contexts (including representation of Martinique at international biennials) get a dedicated gallery presentation in a major European capital. It's a compact but rich introduction to a distinctive voice in postcolonial abstraction.

shows.title: L'Espace entre nous
shows.description:
To mark the bicentennial of photography's invention, Le BAL turns its whole program over to a single private collection for the first time: the Wilson Centre for Photography, assembled over five decades by Michael G. Wilson (the James Bond franchise's longtime producer) and his wife Jane. The roughly 120 prints on view, mostly vintage, span the 1920s to the present and include work by André Kertész, Dorothea Lange, Robert Mapplethorpe, Daidō Moriyama, Weegee and Chris Killip, among some thirty photographers.

Curators Diane Dufour and Julie Héraut organize the material around a single question: what happens in the space between the person photographing and the person photographed. The hang moves along a spectrum from total complicity — portraits made with a subject's full collaboration — to images stolen on the fly, without consent or even awareness, tracing every degree of trust, distance and power in between. It's a smart curatorial device for a collection this eclectic, giving otherwise disparate decades and geographies a shared throughline.

Given the Wilson collection's depth and its rare public exposure, this is a genuine occasion for anyone serious about the history of documentary and portrait photography — a chance to see canonical images alongside more obscure finds, all organized around one of photography's oldest and least resolved questions.

shows.title: Interior Lift 90s
shows.description:
A brief pop-up in Polka's Marais space, Interior Lift 90s gathers Nathaniel Aron's images of domestic and found interiors from the 1990s — a decade whose textures (beige carpets, boxy furniture, fluorescent light) are just far enough away now to read as period detail rather than background noise. Aron's photographs linger on the ordinary rooms and thresholds of that moment, treating them with the same documentary attention that Polka's program usually reserves for reportage and photojournalism.

Shown for only five days, the exhibition works more like a quick, focused capsule than a full retrospective survey — a chance to see a body of work built around a very specific, unglamorous slice of recent visual history before it comes down.

shows.title: 'An Incomplete Survey on Portraiture'. Vol. 2
shows.artist: Kelly Akashi, Marc Asekhame and Taylor Thoroski, Christophe Hamaide Pierson, Assume Vivid Astro Focus, Fabienne Audéoud, H.M. Baker, Stefania Batoeva, Costanza Candeloro, Drake Richard Carr, Shannon Cartier Lucy, Désirée Nakouzi de Monte & Andrea Parenti, Stephan Dillemuth, Ana Viktoria Dziniz, Pé Ferreira, Nicole Gravier, Dario Guccio, Sunil Gupta, Samuel Haitz, Graham Hamilton, Nina Kettiger, Isaac Lythgoe, Miltos Manetas, Emanuele Marcuccio, Sabina Mirri, Raffaela Naldi Rossano, Martin d'Orgeval, Vincenzo Ottino, Matthew Peers, Cameron Platter, Tobias Rehberger, Winnie Mo Rielly, Will Sheridan Jr., Tobias Spichtig, Timothy Lee Standring, Konrad Zukowski
shows.description:
Organized under the curatorial banner "toto," this second volume of An Incomplete Survey on Portraiture crams more than thirty artists into the gallery's main space, treating the portrait not as a fixed genre but as a pretext for wildly different strategies of picturing a self. The checklist ranges from established names like Tobias Rehberger and Kelly Akashi to younger and less-classifiable practices, spanning painting, sculpture, photography, assemblage, and installation.

What holds the show together is less style than premise: every work claims some relationship to a face, a body, or an identity, then proceeds to treat that claim loosely. Installation views show a dense, salon-style hang, with sculptural objects like Graham Hamilton's laserjet-print-and-glass-vase assemblage Reproduction sitting alongside more conventional figurative paintings and photographic prints, including work by the photographer Sunil Gupta.

As the title admits, this is deliberately partial and additive rather than definitive; "Vol. 2" implies a Vol. 3 down the line. The pleasure of the show is in its refusal to resolve into a single argument about what portraiture is for now, instead offering a crowded, generous sampling of contemporary answers to an old question.

shows.title: Tendre Brute: Montessori On Speed
shows.artist: Christophe Hamaide-Pierson and Tor Erik Bøe
shows.description:
Christophe Hamaide-Pierson and Tor Erik Bøe share the gallery's La Cuisine annex for a two-hander that plays soft materials against hard nerves. The title, Montessori On Speed, pitches childhood pedagogy against a jittery, accelerated present, and the works on view lean into that friction: bright, tactile, almost toy-like objects and images that carry an undertow of anxiety or excess just beneath their playful surfaces.

Hamaide-Pierson has long worked at the edge of craft and kitsch, building sculptural tableaux out of everyday and confectionery-adjacent materials that read as both tender and slightly unsettling. Bøe, a Norwegian painter, brings a looser, more gestural sensibility, his canvases oscillating between figuration and abstraction. Shown together in the intimate La Cuisine space, the two practices amplify each other, turning a small room into a concentrated dose of color, texture, and nervous energy.

It's a compact, unfussy summer show, more experimental annex than headline exhibition, but it rewards a slow look: the installation shots show works crowded close together, inviting comparison between the artists' very different handling of surface and subject.

shows.title: Ce que la lumière n'éclaire plus (What Light No Longer Illuminates)
shows.description:
Vincent Lemaire's third solo exhibition at Galerie Dix9 grew out of a text-based commission: the artist was named a 2025 laureate of the Ekphrasis grant awarded by ADAGP, and this body of work is his visual answer to a piece of writing produced for that prize by critic Léo Marin. The result is less an illustration of the text than a parallel investigation into deep time, matter and the origins of life, carried out through Lemaire's long-running photographic and sculptural vocabulary.

The show brings together several of his ongoing series — Panspermie, Lithopanspermie, Matrice fossile, Matriarches — that treat the photogram and the darkroom print as almost geological processes: light burning traces into paper the way sediment records the passage of time. Alongside straightforward silver prints, Lemaire builds wall pieces that incorporate asphalt, lead, pulleys, rope and broken fluorescent tubes, pushing the photographic image toward sculpture and installation.

It's a quiet, materially dense show that rewards close looking — the pleasure is in the accumulation of textures and the sense of images excavated rather than simply taken. For anyone interested in photography pushed past its usual flatness, this is a good one to catch during its short three-week run.

venue.name: Galerie Dix9 Hélène Lacharmoise
venue.address: 19 rue des Filles du Calvaire, 75003 Paris

shows.title: After The Procession
shows.description:
Bram Kinsbergen paints the moment after the spectacle has passed: empty stages, drifting figures, and half-lit interiors that feel like stills from a film whose plot you never learn. The Belgian painter works in mixed media on linen, building up surfaces that sit somewhere between abstraction and figuration, so that silhouettes and objects seem to surface from, and dissolve back into, the ground they're painted on.

For After The Procession, his fourth solo show with the gallery, Kinsbergen continues to mine memory and the strange residue left by digital images that have been seen, shared, and half-forgotten. Isolated figures, animals, and architectural fragments recur across large canvases, staged in murky, night-lit spaces that recall both history painting and the scroll of a phone screen at 2am.

The title points to what's left over once a public ritual — a parade, a ceremony, a crowd — has moved on: the stragglers, the debris, the after-image. It's a fitting way to describe Kinsbergen's whole project, which treats painting itself as a kind of afterimage of experience, never quite settling into a single, legible scene.

Kinsbergen (b. 1984, Boechout, Belgium) has shown at Everyday Gallery Antwerp, Pal Project Paris, BLANK Gallery Shanghai, and Schunck Heerlen, among others, and this marks his latest presentation with PACT in the Marais.

shows.title: CURSUS / CORPUS
shows.description:
Julie Laporte's first solo show with Galerie Binome treats the photographic darkroom as a site of accident and salvage rather than control. Her materials are the rejects of analog photography itself — oxidized cibachrome ruined by mechanical faults, torn scraps of baryta paper, chemical stains — reassembled into sculptural objects that barely resemble photographs anymore.

The works fall into a few recurring families on view: the Flux pieces, warped cibachrome sheets folded and mounted behind steel and plexiglass like specimens; the Chymères, suspended cocoon-like sculptures built from pulped darkroom paper and wire, more textile or biological form than image; and the AfterGlow and Prismes series, in which lumen prints and multiple exposures produce ghostly color fields with no camera involved at all. Across all of them Laporte treats photographic chemistry as a physical, almost sculptural process — pouring, folding, oxidizing — rather than a means of capturing a scene.

The show is co-curated with collectors Patrice Galiana and Caroline Wiart, and runs as the second half of a two-part project that began at Espace d'art La Moulinette in Montmartre. It's a rewarding show for anyone interested in photography's material edges — where the medium stops describing the world and starts becoming an object in its own right.

shows.title: Robert Frank – Mabou / John Cohen – Pull My Daisy
shows.description:
This two-hander pairs Robert Frank's later photographs made at his home in Mabou, Nova Scotia, with John Cohen's on-set pictures from the 1959 Beat film Pull My Daisy, and in doing so tells a story about friendship as much as about photography. Cohen — folk musician, ethnomusicologist and photographer — was Frank's neighbor in the East Village and was invited onto the set as the film's stills photographer, giving him unusually intimate access to Allen Ginsberg, Jack Kerouac, Gregory Corso, Alfred Leslie and Frank's own family during the shoot.

The Mabou pictures come from the other end of Frank's career, after he had largely turned away from the solitary practice of still photography that produced The Americans and settled into filmmaking and a quieter life in Nova Scotia with his wife June Leaf. Seeing the two bodies of work side by side underlines how much of Frank's photography was really about the people around him — the Beat circle in New York in 1959, and the domestic world of Mabou decades later.

For anyone interested in the Beat Generation's visual record, the Cohen material is the rarer draw: these are not stills in the promotional sense but genuinely observed portraits of a specific, fertile moment in American underground culture, including Delphine Seyrig's first appearance on film. It's a tightly focused, research-driven show rather than a blockbuster, well suited to this photography-specialist gallery in the Marais.

shows.title: Poèmes graphiques
shows.description:
Michel Houellebecq is not a name usually associated with a gallery wall, but this show grows out of a genuine collaboration: architect and illustrator Louis Paillard, who previously adapted Houellebecq's Goncourt-winning novel La Carte et le territoire into graphic-novel form, has spent the past two years turning the writer's poems into drawn images, publishing a chapter each month in the magazine Charlotte. Poèmes graphiques brings the resulting artwork into the gallery, timed to a forthcoming book collecting the series.

The poems themselves span several of Houellebecq's collections — La poursuite du bonheur, Renaissance, Configuration du dernier rivage — filtered through Paillard's direct, flatly colored linework, which sits somewhere between comic strip and illustrated broadside. The pairing plays up the deadpan, melancholic humor that runs through Houellebecq's verse as much as his novels, giving it a visual register it hasn't had before.

It's an unusual entry in Romero Paprocki's program, less a conventional painting or photography show than a display of an ongoing literary-visual project — worth a look for Houellebecq's admirers and for anyone curious what his particular strain of resigned, generation-X sarcasm looks like translated into pictures.

shows.title: Almageste
shows.description:
Named after Ptolemy's Almagest — the ancient treatise that once mapped the visible sky — this summer-long photography exhibition takes on the canal-side art center's warehouse walls with a body of work oriented, in spirit if not always literally, toward looking upward: light, distance, and the way images try to fix things that are essentially in motion.

Point Éphémère has run a photography show through its summer programming for years now, using the gap between its regular concert and residency schedule to give its walls over to a single sustained body of work rather than the one-night events that otherwise fill its calendar. Almageste fits that slot, on view for over ten weeks alongside the venue's usual run of concerts, club nights, and festival programming.

Given the venue's alternative, artist-run character, don't expect a white cube presentation — this is photography seen in a raw industrial space that doubles as a bar, a rehearsal studio, and a stage, which is part of the appeal for anyone who wants to catch it on the way to a show.

shows.title: Even as They Fade
shows.description:
Installed in the street-level Vitrine of the Cité internationale des arts' Marais site, this is a slow-motion unmaking. Tokyo-born artist Sakura Momma — trained in embroidery at Paris's École Lesage and in intermedia art at Tokyo University of the Arts — has stretched a transparent voile of organza across the window, every inch of it hand-embroidered with glass beads. A mechanical device tugs steadily at the thread over the course of the installation's run, unpicking the stitching bead by bead so that what was painstakingly sewn slowly comes undone in public view.

The piece is less an object than a duration: because the fabric is transparent, it never resolves into a legible "finished" image, and its changes only become visible through attention — the click of a falling bead, a shift of light, a change in the viewer's own position. Momma has spoken of wanting to make visible the invisible labor accumulated in every stitch, and the piece's title captures that ambivalence: nothing here is destroyed, exactly, only relocated, its visibility and function continually changing.

It's a quiet, conceptually tight work well suited to a passerby's glance from the street as much as a longer look, and its final day (September 9) doubles as a participatory closing event, where visitors are invited to bring a soft object or worn garment for the artist to stitch with beads that fell during the installation's run.

shows.title: Une fenêtre contre le temps (A Window Against Time)
shows.description:
This show closes out Drawing Factory II, a six-month residency that put fifteen artists to work in a shared building at 61 Rue de Richelieu, by moving their output next door into the Drawing Hotel and into Drawing Lab itself. Curator Claire Luna treats "drawing" in its most elastic sense: a line, a gesture, a video, a smell, a piece of furniture, anything that carries the trace of a hand and a period of shared, quiet attention.

Rather than a conventional hang, the works infiltrate the hotel's actual functions — a mood report standing in for the weather on the café television, a strange geological-looking loaf turning up at random on breakfast plates, ants parading across a library shelf, a single guest room made inhabitable for one night by an artist's intervention. The effect is less an exhibition to look at than an atmosphere to notice, built from small disruptions to ordinary hospitality.

The fifteen participants — among them Amélie Barnathan, Tamaris Borrelly, Marguerite Canguilhem, Louise Dumas, Justine Joly, Boryana Petkova and Adji Titus — represent a cross-section of a younger generation of artists trained or based in Paris, most showing publicly for the first time since their residency. It's a modest, unhurried show, and it closes within days, so this is very much a last-chance visit before Drawing Lab turns to its next, more historically-minded project.

shows.title: Virgin Turns (Virages Vierges)
shows.description:
Pauline Curnier Jardin builds immersive, slightly unhinged worlds out of video, fabric sculpture and performance, and this survey at Palais de Tokyo is the biggest showcase of her work to date in France. The title plays on a double meaning: virgins as female bodies loaded with centuries of sanctification and suspicion, saints and sinners at once, and virgin territory as unmapped ground where new stories can take root. Both readings run through the show's tented, womb-like installations and looping video works, where ritual, camp theatrics and documentary footage bleed into each other without much regard for hierarchy.

The centerpiece is a new video installation inspired by a real clandestine cinema discovered in 2004 in tunnels beneath the Trocadéro, practically underneath the museum itself, a detail that gives the whole show a nice sense of digging into buried, dissident histories literally on its own doorstep. Elsewhere, large fabric structures recall crumbling amphitheaters and reliquaries, staging her recurring interest in bodily vulnerability, popular spirituality and the theater of femininity.

Curnier Jardin has been circling these ideas for years in group shows at Palais de Tokyo and in major presentations at Hamburger Bahnhof and elsewhere, but Virgin Turns is her fullest statement yet, and it's being organized in partnership with the Reina Sofía in Madrid, which will host its own version in 2027. It's an odd, immersive, occasionally overwhelming show, well suited to a museum that has always made room for art on the edge of spectacle.

shows.title: Les Chiens de Pavlov (Pavlov's Dogs)
shows.description:
Johan Creten has spent nearly forty years reestablishing ceramics as a serious contemporary medium, working his way through studios in Mexico, Rome, Miami and The Hague before settling into La Solfatara, the shared Montreuil studio he keeps with Jean-Michel Othoniel. This new show at Perrotin's Marais space starts from an unusually personal object: a stack of obsolete computer towers inherited from his father, a lifelong devotee of new technology, which Creten piles up like ruins and treats as a monument to a certain kind of faith in progress that has visibly aged.

Around that installation, the exhibition fills out with the vocabulary Creten is best known for: glazed stoneware and bronze creatures, drawings, and recurring figures like his condor and Danaé, cast here in new material or new scale. The title nods to Pavlov's conditioning experiments, and Creten uses it to prod at reflex and automatism, how quickly certain images or objects trigger a response before we've thought about why. A section given over to the seven virtues slows the pace back down, working as counterweight to the show's more anxious, tech-fossil energy.

It's a free, walk-in show and a good entry point into Creten's work if you don't know it: playful in material, but with real unease underneath about memory, obsolescence, and what we choose to keep believing in.

shows.title: Mémoire Matérielle
shows.artist: Gaëlle Choisne, Joana Choumali, Andile Dyalvane, Carla Gueye
shows.description:
Four artists share a conviction that the hand is a form of thinking: this show gathers coil-built ceramics, embroidered photographs, cast and accumulated sculpture, and a room-scale installation of salvaged materials, all bound by processes that take time and leave visible traces of labor. Andile Dyalvane's ceramic vessels carry the scarified surface language of amaXhosa ritual objects; Joana Choumali continues her signature practice of stitching directly into photographic prints, turning embroidery into a slow act of repair and remembrance; Carla Gueye builds sculptural surfaces through touch and accretion; and 2024 Prix Marcel Duchamp laureate Gaëlle Choisne expands the show into installation, working with reclaimed matter tied to Creole and Franco-Haitian histories.

Curated by Azu Nwagbogu and Nkhensani Mkhari, the exhibition takes as its intellectual anchor the Martinican theorist Paulette Nardal's 1930s writing on memory as something built rather than simply inherited — a labor of reconstruction rather than nostalgia. That framework gives the show its throughline: each artist treats craft and material process (clay, thread, cast metal, found objects) as a way of holding onto ancestral and personal history that colonial modernity tried to sever.

Visitors can expect a quietly physical exhibition — heavy with texture, slow to read, and more interested in the residue of making than in finished spectacle. It's a strong choice for anyone curious about how contemporary African and diaspora artists are using traditional hand-craft vocabularies (coiled ceramics, embroidery, assemblage) to make arguments about history and inheritance.

shows.title: Nos géographies intimes (Our Intimate Geographies)
shows.description:
Hervé Yamguen's second solo show at AFIKARIS brings together drawings, paintings, bronze sculpture, and wooden masks built around a single question: what makes up a person beyond what's visible? Yamguen, who is also a poet and a notable within his home chiefdom in Cameroon, treats faces, trees, birds, and hybrid figures as vessels for accumulated experience — places lived in, ancestors carried forward, seasons that mark a body the way they mark a tree.

The bronzes are cast using the lost-wax technique in Foumban, putting an old regional craft in direct conversation with Yamguen's contemporary drawing and painting practice; works on paper and canvas extend into volume and back again, as if the same image kept changing material. Thematically the show leans on Ubuntu philosophy and animist thought — the idea that a person is never separate from ancestors, land, or the non-human world — rather than presenting identity as fixed or singular.

It's a good entry point for anyone interested in contemporary Central African sculpture and drawing that stays close to spoken and sung tradition without illustrating it literally; Yamguen's figures are layered and unresolved by design, closer to accumulation than portraiture.

shows.title: Sfondo
shows.description:
Pauline Bazignan's first solo show at Backslash keeps her long-running dialogue with Italian Renaissance painting but redirects it toward a single, oddly specific target: the landscape behind the Mona Lisa. Rather than copying Leonardo's figure, Bazignan tries to reconstruct the strange background terrain that surrounds her, building the compositions in successive painted layers and then letting water dissolve and drag parts of the pigment away — a controlled-accident process that produces her own version of sfumato, somewhere between appearance and erasure.

The Mona Lisa herself surfaces only faintly across the paintings, more felt than seen, while the horizon and rock formations behind her become the real subject. The show also includes sculptures from Bazignan's recurring series, cast in the same misty blues and earth tones as the paintings, plus an opening diptych inspired by Paolo Uccello's Battle of San Romano that bridges her previous body of work with this new one.

Bazignan trained at the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Paris and has shown at institutions including the Musée d'Art Moderne de Fontevraud and the Villa Datris Foundation; this is a good show for anyone interested in contemporary painters working through — rather than against — the most over-reproduced image in Western art.

shows.title: Essence
shows.description:
Morgan Courtois works mainly in cast and carved sculpture, often in materials — soap, resin, plaster — that carry a built-in fragility or a suggestion of the body's own softness and impermanence. "Essence" is his second show at Balice Hertling since his 2016 debut there, following a run of institutional presentations that include the Fondation Pernod Ricard and the Centre d'art contemporain Les Capucins.

Courtois's figures tend to hover between the classical and the eroded: torsos, faces, and hands that look excavated or half-dissolved rather than modeled, as if sculpture here is as much about material loss as about form. Given the show's title, expect a body of work that strips its subjects down toward something closer to residue or essence than to finished portraiture.

It's a compact but focused show worth catching for anyone interested in contemporary approaches to figurative sculpture that lean into decay and unstable material rather than permanence.

shows.title: Catching Forms. Wood to Bronze
shows.description:
David Nash has spent five decades working directly with felled and salvaged timber, letting the character of each piece of wood — how it splits, how it dries, its inherent volume — guide the sculpture that emerges. This show tracks a parallel practice he's developed more recently: casting those wood forms into bronze, translating something perishable and organic into something durable.

The pivot point, literally and conceptually, was Inside/Outside (2011), where Nash cast the negative space chainsawed out of a tree stump — turning a void into a solid form. A larger version, Night Form (2026), anchors this exhibition alongside sculptures like the Celtic Column and Cross Column, pieces first developed as wood in his converted-chapel studio in Wales before being reworked and cast. The bronzes carry the memory of their wooden origins in their surfaces, some finished black to mimic charred wood, others taking on green, brown or red patinas that pull them further from their source material.

It's a good entry point into Nash's practice for anyone who knows him primarily as a wood sculptor — the bronzes make the underlying logic of his working method, catching and fixing a form, unusually legible, precisely because the material has changed but the gesture hasn't.

shows.title: Pineta
shows.description:
For twenty years Fabienne Verdier has returned each summer to the Bay of Porto Vecchio in Corsica, and this show is essentially a distillation of that repeated looking. Working in dry pastel for rock and stone and oil pastel for the gnarled pine trunks, she renders the headlands, coves and horizon lines of the coast in spare, almost sculptural marks — drawings that feel closer to carving than mark-making.

The restraint is the point: a single collaged sheet of blue paper stands in for the sea's flatness, and the pastel strokes leave enough white space that the works ask to be read as much through absence as through line. It's a sensory approach to landscape that trades detail for something closer to atmosphere — the scent of resin, the sound of wind through needles — built from a place Verdier clearly knows intimately rather than one she's visiting as a subject.

Verdier's reputation was built on her calligraphic abstraction, developed after years of training in China, and this Corsican series shows that same disciplined, gestural hand turned toward a specific, real landscape rather than pure abstraction — a useful show for seeing how her formal vocabulary adapts when there's an actual place behind it.

shows.title: How Do You Even Sleep At Night?
shows.description:
Wallen Mapondera has built his reputation on sculptural assemblages made from cardboard, packaging and repurposed textiles — materials that carry the economic history of everyday survival in Zimbabwe. This third solo show with the gallery marks a genuine pivot: a body of new paintings that extends his long-running interest in informal trade and state power into a more traditional medium.

The title poses a blunt moral question, and it comes from a personal source — the seizure of goods belonging to the artist's sister, who runs a clothing business, by Zimbabwean authorities acting within the letter of the law. From that specific injury, Mapondera opens onto broader questions about the distance between administrative decisions and the people who absorb their consequences, and about where responsibility lands when an action is legal but experienced as unjust.

It's a show that trades the physical density of his collage work for the more direct address of painting, without losing the social specificity that's always anchored his practice. Worth catching for anyone who's followed his material-based work and wants to see how the same concerns translate onto canvas.

shows.title: MP#06
shows.artist: Jennifer Carlos, Judith Crico, Tavan Esmaili, Léa Pignard, Adrien Viot
shows.description:
This is the graduation show for the sixth cohort of the Fonds Régnier pour la Création's photography mentorship program, run with Agence VU'. Five emerging photographers — Jennifer Carlos, Judith Crico, Tavan Esmaili, Léa Pignard and Adrien Viot — spent nine months in a structured program of mentorship, expert consultations, professional training and collective workshops, and this exhibition is the visible result of that process.

Because it's a mentorship cohort rather than a curated theme show, the work on view spans a real range of approaches and subjects, which makes it a useful snapshot of where younger French documentary and art photography is right now rather than a single argument about it. The gallery also folds in a small selection of prints from the Laurence Régnier private collection, giving visitors a chance to see the five years of the mentorship program (2020–2025) in wider context.

It's a low-key but genuinely useful show for anyone interested in how photography gets professionalized and mentored in France today — less about masterworks than about process, and about a handful of photographers worth watching going forward.

shows.title: Christian Marclay
shows.description:
Christian Marclay has spent decades treating recorded sound as sculptural raw material, and this show turns his attention specifically to the record sleeve — the printed cardboard jacket that protects and advertises a vinyl LP, rather than the disc itself. In a new body of monotypes, he inks paper sleeves and covers in 7", 10" and 12" formats and transfers their surfaces directly onto paper, so that every crease, tear and handling mark left by decades of use becomes part of the final image.

A parallel series called "Oculi" pushes the same material further: Marclay collages vintage sleeves whose circular die-cut windows — originally there to show off the spinning label underneath — become framing devices for isolated fragments of the imagery beneath, a pair of eyes, a mouth, a hand caught mid-gesture. The effect turns cover art designed for quick recognition on a record store shelf into something closer to a cropped, uncanny portrait.

It's a tightly focused, materially inventive show from an artist best known for large-scale sound works and video, here working small and quiet with found ephemera. For anyone who has ever lingered over the graphic design of an old record cover, there's real pleasure in watching Marclay dissect that object down to its printed skin.

shows.title: I am Fine: What Woman Wants — Portraits, Figures and Fictions of Femininity
shows.description:
Drawing entirely from the gallery's own collection, this group show gathers a roster of urban-art and street-art-adjacent names — Vhils, YZ, Shepard Fairey, Liu Bolin, Mark Jenkins, André Saraiva, Zevs — alongside painters and sculptors like Cécile Cornet, Rakajoo, Prune Nourry, and FaithXLVII to interrogate how the female figure gets built, worn, and sometimes torn down by the gaze of others. The show's anchor is a Niels "Shoe" Meulman piece: an antique-looking mirror engraved with the phrase "I AM FINE" in calligraphic script, legible only when a viewer's own reflection lines up with the words — so that every visitor becomes, willingly or not, part of the work.

The exhibition moves through a loose narrative arc: it opens on faces (YZ's crowned "Empresses," Erwin Olaf's staged interiors) that stage the tension between woman-as-icon and woman-as-subject, then turns to artists reclaiming their own image — Cornet's scarred, painted bodies passed mother to daughter, Nourry's invented army of "Terracotta Daughters" filling a historical void, Xi Song's papier-mâché spheres built from secondhand books. A second current runs through works that show the female figure being manufactured or erased from outside: Vhils's carved-away faces surfacing from torn advertising posters, Zevs's vandalized fashion billboards, Rakajoo's quietly tense waiting-room portraits.

It's a broad, collection-based survey rather than a single curatorial thesis, but the range is real — from calligraphy and photography to embroidery, carved posters, and street sculpture — and the checklist brings together some genuinely major names in contemporary urban art under a theme with sharper edges than the pun in the title suggests.

shows.title: Au 108 rue Vieille du Temple: A Shared Legacy with Galerie Yvon Lambert
shows.description:
Forty years after Yvon Lambert inaugurated his gallery at 108 rue Vieille du Temple with a Cy Twombly show, David Zwirner marks the anniversary with a group exhibition that treats the address itself as the subject. Lambert ran his program here for nearly three decades before Zwirner took over the space in 2019, and this show threads together thirty-two artists who passed through one or both eras — a rare instance of a gallery building an exhibition around its own site's institutional memory rather than a single artist or theme.

The checklist reads like a survey of postwar conceptual and minimal art crossed with the painters and photographers who gave the program its later range: Twombly, On Kawara, Richard Serra, and Sol LeWitt (who had fifteen solo shows with Lambert) anchor the historical through-line, while Basquiat's "Red Joy," Barbara Kruger's confrontational text pieces, Nan Goldin's photographs, and Bruce Nauman's cast bronze hands broaden it into painting, photography, and sculpture. More recent work by Nathalie du Pasquier and Robert Combas keeps the show from reading purely as archival tribute.

What makes the exhibition worth seeing isn't just the individual pieces but the curatorial premise: wall texts and archival ephemera (show cards, invites designed by LeWitt and Weiner) trace the gallery's own exhibition history at this specific address, turning the show into a compact history of how postwar American art reached Paris audiences through one influential dealer's eye — and how that legacy directly shaped the program that occupies the space today.

shows.title: Les oranges
shows.description:
Elvire Bonduelle returns to Double V's Paris space with "Les oranges," a new solo exhibition of paintings following her recent shows in Marseille and at Art-O-Rama. Bonduelle's work has long circled the textures of everyday domestic and bodily life — food, skin, still life motifs rendered with a loose, saturated hand — and the citrus of the title suggests another close, almost tactile study of ordinary things made strange through color and paint handling.

Based on the works on view, expect bright, high-keyed canvases where fruit, flesh, and interior scenes blur into one another, continuing a practice that has made Bonduelle one of the more distinctive colorists on the current French painting scene. Her pictures tend to hover between figuration and abstraction, holding onto just enough recognizable form — a curve, a rind, a shadow — to keep the eye anchored while the paint itself does something looser and more instinctive.

This is Bonduelle's latest outing with a gallery that has represented her for several years and given her a steady platform across both its Paris and Marseille spaces, making it a good chance to track how her handling of color and everyday subject matter has developed over a run of closely spaced exhibitions.

shows.title: Je suis une économie du désir (I Am an Economy of Desire)
shows.description:
Sarah Tritz fills the gallery with an odd procession: scale models of heavy-duty lorries lined up along the walls, earthenware dinosaurs keeping them company, and sketches of airplanes — drawn on paper deliberately aged and yellowed — raining down from above. Some planes crash, some take off; the trucks and dinosaurs simply keep moving forward. It's a tableau built from mismatched registers of memory, toy-like in scale but heavy with implication.

Tritz has described the dinosaurs in the show as a child's half-remembered composite of an extinct species — a drawing reconstructed from fragments of many "sub-species" that got flattened, in memory, into a single creature called "dinosaur." That slippage between what's recalled and what's real runs through the whole installation: the trucks stand in for the history of commerce and of men, the dinosaurs for a deeper, more mythic history, and somewhere between them, per the artist, sits the unwritten history of women and of children — a category Tritz pointedly suggests may not exist as cleanly as we assume.

The result is less a show about objects than about the "economy" of desire itself: memory, transport, and the small spaces where things are held before they disappear. It's a quietly strange, materially playful body of work from an artist known for treating everyday and toy-scaled objects as vessels for bigger, more ambiguous historical and psychological freight — worth seeing for anyone drawn to sculpture that thinks through miniature form rather than monumental gesture.

shows.title: Predizione Perdizione
shows.description:
João Vilhena continues his Predizione Perdizione series with a third chapter, following presentations in Venice and at the Palais Fesch in Ajaccio. The Paris installment brings together a group of large-scale drawings made in black chalk on grey cardboard, a deliberately humble, matte medium that Vilhena has made his signature over the past decade.

The drawings work through fragments of historical imagery — figures, monuments, scenes that read as excavated from an archive of collective memory — and set them against the artist's own contemporary anxieties. The result is less a narrative than a mood: a slow-burning meditation on prediction and loss (the title translates roughly as "prediction, perdition") that treats drawing as a way of processing what feels historically inevitable.

Vilhena works at a scale that pushes the intimacy of chalk drawing toward something closer to history painting, and the grey cardboard support keeps the palette almost monochrome, all the more dramatic for its restraint. It's a compact, focused show, well suited to a first look at an artist whose vocabulary of stark figuration and worn materials is gaining international attention.

shows.title: Arrière-train fantôme (Ghost Rump)
shows.description:
Marie Losier is best known internationally as a filmmaker — her portraits of outsider musicians and performers (Genesis P-Orridge, Guy Maddin's circle, the duo Arlt) have played festivals worldwide — but this show turns to the drawing, collage, and textile work that runs alongside her films. Pen, watercolor, and collage on paper sit next to sewn and screen-printed fabric pieces, all made with the same restless, handmade energy as her moving-image work.

The pieces on view read like stills pulled from an imaginary film: costumed figures, fetish objects, and fairground imagery rendered in loose, confident line and wet color. Losier has described her practice as one long act of mythologizing the people around her — friends, lovers, chosen family — turning them into recurring characters in a private cosmology, and that same impulse animates the works here, several of which involve close collaborators like the musician Sing Sing (of the band Arlt).

It's a modest-scaled, intimate show, heavy on paper and fabric rather than spectacle, and it rewards close looking — the kind of exhibition where the wall texts (Losier's own writing is characteristically playful and strange) are as worth reading as the images are worth studying.

shows.title: Pluie Fossile
shows.description:
Julien Discrit works at the intersection of stone and data in this show, carving marble the way sculptors have for millennia while feeding it content generated by algorithms and old film scripts. The title, "Fossil Rain," sets the tone: this is an exhibition about how memory gets deposited, layer by layer, in materials that outlast the people who made them.

The centerpiece is a series called Engrammes — marble slabs engraved with fragmentary sentences that read like diary entries or half-remembered dreams ("the smell comes back on the first street, everything's smaller than before"). Discrit calls them "engrams," borrowing the neuroscience term for a physical trace of memory in the brain, and here that trace becomes literal: words cut into stone, permanent where memory itself is not. Alongside them are the sculptural Embrace works, softly rounded marble forms that read as abstracted gestures of holding on.

A parallel body of work, Tears in Rain, takes its title from the Blade Runner replicant monologue about memories "lost like tears in rain," and generates chromatographic ink patterns on silica plates — each one named for a fictional life invented by an algorithm, its supposed key memories plotted as points on an invisible grid. It's a strange, poetic pairing: the oldest sculptural material there is, marked by the newest tools for manufacturing false histories. The show asks what happens to memory when both stone and software can be made to hold it.

shows.title: Glade / Clairière
shows.description:
Wolfgang Tillmans returns to Galerie Chantal Crousel a year after his sprawling Centre Pompidou retrospective closed, and after a year spent as a visiting professor at the Beaux-Arts de Paris. Glade / Clairière is built around a motif the gallery describes as central to his recent work: the line, sometimes drawn and deliberate, sometimes found in the world and simply recorded, running through his photographs as a thread between control and chance.

Tillmans has spent over three decades refusing to settle into a single photographic register — club culture and portraiture sit alongside still lifes, astronomical images, and near-abstractions made through direct manipulation of photographic paper — and this show continues that restlessness rather than resolving it. Expect large-scale prints alongside more intimate works, installed in the loose, non-hierarchical hang that has become one of his own signatures as much as any single image.

As the first photographer and first non-British artist to win the Turner Prize, and with major surveys behind him at Tate, MoMA, and now the Pompidou, Tillmans hardly needs introduction — but a gallery show like this one, scaled to a single space rather than a museum floor, is where his eye for sequencing and juxtaposition is easiest to see up close.

shows.title: Les objecteurs (The Objectors)
shows.description:
Sixty years ago the critic Alain Jouffroy staged a three-gallery Paris event called "Les Objecteurs," pulling together Arman, Tetsumi Kudo, Daniel Pommereulle, Jean-Pierre Raynaud, and Daniel Spoerri under a shared idea: that everyday objects, rather than paint or bronze, could carry thought itself, functioning as provocations rather than as sculpture or parody-painting. Galerie Christophe Gaillard restages that premise for its own space, pairing historical works by Kudo and Pommereulle with a wider group spanning several generations of French object-based art.

The show adds artists of the confirmed postwar generation — Pierre Ardouvin, Eric Baudart, Anita Molinero — whose practices pick up Jouffroy's original argument in different registers: Molinero's scorched and melted industrial plastics (roadside bins, car parts, foam) read the built environment's castoffs as a form of social diagnosis, while Baudart's spare rearrangements of ordinary objects quietly destabilize how familiar things are perceived. A younger generation, represented by David Douard and Mimosa Echard, pushes the object further toward hybrid, almost organic territory — assemblages that mix street debris, technology, and biological or botanical material until the categories blur.

It's a smart piece of historical restaging rather than a straightforward group show: less about any single artist than about tracing a sixty-year lineage of French artists who treat the object, not the image, as the basic unit of thought. Kudo's boxed, dice-like symbolic objects and Pommereulle's charged combinations of blades and found forms anchor the show in its 1960s origins, while the contemporary works make the case that the "objector" impulse never really went away.

shows.title: le flâneur
shows.description:
Jacques Villeglé (1926–2022) made a career out of walking Paris and peeling advertising posters straight off the walls, then presenting the torn, layered, weather-beaten results as finished works — the "affiches lacérées" that made him one of the founding figures of Nouveau Réalisme. "le flâneur" leans into that identity: the show is built around the idea of the artist as urban wanderer, collecting the city's accidental collages rather than inventing his own compositions.

The works on view are named, as Villeglé always named them, for the streets and dates where he tore them down — a poster lifted from the Rue du Théâtre in January 1961, stickers pulled from the Boulevard Saint-Martin in 1978, layers gathered on the Rue du Temple and the Rue Claude Vellefaux. Seen together, they read as a kind of alternative cartography of postwar Paris, each sheet carrying the overlapping graphic noise — typography, color, tears, glue — of whatever campaigns and slogans happened to compete for that particular wall.

There's a deceptively simple pleasure in these pieces: they look like abstraction, but every mark in them was made by someone else, and Villeglé's only intervention was choosing where to cut. Decades on, they still feel like some of the freshest, least mannered gestures to come out of that generation of French art, and this focused hang is a good primer on why he's remained a reference point for artists working with appropriation and the urban surface.

shows.title: Trafic – Hommage à Peter Stämpfli
shows.artist: Eulàlia Grau, Peter Halley, Emanuel Proweller, Daniel Spoerri, Peter Stämpfli, Jacques Villeglé
shows.description:
This group show at the gallery's 33 Rue de Seine space pays tribute to Peter Stämpfli, the Swiss painter best known for his hyperreal, cropped close-ups of tires and racing-car bodywork, by putting him in dialogue with other artists who have made speed, circulation and the imagery of the road part of their vocabulary. It's a loose but coherent premise: traffic as both literal subject and a metaphor for how images and objects move and collide.

Alongside Stämpfli's own tightly rendered tire and car paintings, the show brings in Daniel Spoerri's object-based assemblages, Peter Halley's hard-edged geometric abstractions (themselves indebted to circuitry and infrastructure imagery), Emanuel Proweller's mid-century abstraction, Eulàlia Grau's collage-based social critique, and Jacques Villeglé's torn-poster works — a fitting overlap with his concurrent solo show at the gallery's other space nearby.

It's an unusual pairing of generations and geographies, held together less by shared style than by a common interest in the urban object as raw material, and it gives Stämpfli — a figure sometimes overshadowed by his American Pop contemporaries — a chance to be seen in a wider, more international context of postwar art dealing with mechanization and speed.

shows.title: La Mue
shows.description:
Tessa Mars is a Haitian painter whose work has long circled around a recurring alter ego, Manman Zombi, through whom she explores self-image, Vodou cosmology and the layered colonial and postcolonial history written onto Haitian bodies and land. "La Mue" — literally "the molt" or "the shedding" — points to a show built around transformation: the shedding of skin, of imposed identity, of inherited narrative.

Given the title and Mars's established visual language, expect paintings that stage the body mid-transition, using the vivid color and flattened, folkloric figuration she's known for to suggest metamorphosis rather than a fixed, single self-portrait. Her work consistently treats the personal and the political as inseparable, using her own image as a site where questions of gender, race and national history get worked out in paint.

This is Galerie Imane Farès continuing a program built around artists from the Caribbean, Middle East and African diaspora, and Tessa Mars's first solo outing with the gallery — a good introduction to an artist whose reputation has been building steadily since her early exhibitions in Port-au-Prince and the Caribbean biennial circuit.

shows.title: Au fil de l'eau
