shows.description:
Elizabeth Garouste has spent four decades refusing to sit still inside the category of "designer," even though her Barbare chair with the late Mattia Bonetti became one of the defining objects of 1980s French design. Since going solo she's leaned harder into a personal, almost folkloric visual language built from masks, hand-worked bronze and iron, textiles and drawing. This second solo show with Ketabi Bourdet gathers new work around water — the sea, its creatures, its endless capacity for transformation.

Expect the full range of her practice in one room: sculptural furniture and lighting alongside masks built up from plaster bandaging, wrought-iron consoles and mirrors, tapestries, and the loose, naive-inflected drawings she treats as a kind of daily notation. Her forms — heads, faces, animal-hybrid creatures — sit somewhere between art brut and decorative art, refusing the line the market usually tries to draw between the two.

At nearly eighty, Garouste shows no sign of repeating herself, and this gallery — which pairs contemporary art with historically significant design — is a fitting home for work that has always insisted the two were never really separate. Given the show's marine theme, it should read as looser and more atmospheric than her furniture-focused outings, closer to an installation than a showroom.

shows.title: Anthem
shows.description:
Anthem is Yasuko Hirano's first exhibition with galerie frank elbaz, bringing together recent abstract paintings built from oil, plaster and glue worked into canvas over wooden panels. The surfaces are thick and worked-over, with the plaster giving the paint a chalky, excavated quality — closer to a wall that's been through several rounds of repair than a conventional painted canvas.

Hirano's abstraction keeps circling back to memory, repetition and mental landscape rather than pure formal concerns; the paintings read as records of returning to the same gesture or mark again and again, each pass slightly different from the last. That repetition-as-renewal idea is central to how she talks about her own process — treating painting not as a way of preserving something fixed from the past but as a live encounter that keeps producing new time with each iteration.

For a first Paris gallery show, Anthem is a strong, cohesive introduction: the palette stays close and earthbound, the surfaces reward close viewing, and the whole body of work has the patient, accretive feel of an artist who has been refining a single idea carefully rather than chasing variety.

shows.title: Earth and Sky
shows.description:
Sungi Mlengeya's first monographic exhibition in France arrives as an extension of a signature approach: figures rendered in warm, richly modeled brown tones that seem to float free of any background, the white of the raw canvas standing in for space itself. Bodies emerge mid-gesture, limbs and torsos caught in movement, with everything extraneous around them simply left unpainted.

Titled Earth and Sky, the new body of work turns toward questions of continuity, how a life persists past the point of loss, through memory, inheritance and influence passed between generations. It's a quieter, more reflective register than pure portraiture, using the same pared-back visual language the Tanzanian artist has built her reputation on to think about what remains when someone is gone.

The absence of setting is the whole point: without floor, wall or horizon to anchor them, Mlengeya's figures read as archetypal rather than particular, standing in for a broader meditation on transmission and legacy rather than any single story.

shows.title: We Cannot Stop the Birds of Misfortune From Flying Over Our Heads, But Perhaps We Can Stop Them From Nesting There
shows.description:
Qi Zhuo's new solo show takes its title from a well-worn Chinese proverb about misfortune, but treats the phrase less as consolation than as a working method, a way of handling materials, history and the body without pretending bad luck can be avoided altogether. The works on view, including the bulbous, taut Bubble-Game paintings and the more precarious Balancing Ball pieces, translate that idea into forms that look perpetually on the verge of losing their composure.

There's a tension throughout between control and collapse: surfaces stretched tight, rounded volumes that seem inflated to their limit, objects balanced in ways that look temporary rather than resolved. It's a physical, almost bodily vocabulary, closer to sculpture-as-tension than to straightforward object-making.

Staged at the gallery's second Paris space on rue Chapon, opened in 2023 to expand its program, the show gives Zhuo's restless, unresolved forms room to breathe on their own rather than sharing the spotlight with a second artist.

venue.name: Galerie Les Filles du Calvaire (Chapon annex)

shows.title: Les Commensaux
shows.description:
José Loureiro's third solo show at the gallery centers on a new series of oils on canvas and paper that stage odd, half-organic forms in perpetual friction with one another. Bodies that read as humanoid one moment and purely abstract the next crowd the picture plane, bumping, merging and pulling apart in compositions that never quite settle into a single register.

The title, "Les Commensaux" (dinner companions), plays on the double life of the French word "table": both a piece of furniture and the site of shared meals. Recurring motifs of toothy little mouths, cutlery-like sticks, and tubular polychrome forms that seem to dissolve at one end tie the paintings to ideas of eating, hosting and coexistence, sometimes convivial, sometimes closer to friction or predation. It's a loud, heterogeneous body of work, deliberately mixing smooth hard-edged passages with loose, expressive brushwork, geometry with gesture.

Loureiro, a major figure in Portuguese painting who recently had a large-scale retrospective spread across three floors of the Frac Grand Large in Dunkirk, has spent decades pushing a minimalist grid vocabulary toward increasingly strange, animate territory; Les Commensaux continues that trajectory, treating heterogeneity itself as the subject rather than a stylistic tic.

shows.title: Ferdinandea
shows.description:
Clément Cogitore's first solo exhibition with the gallery takes its name from a phantom island: Ferdinandea, a volcanic outcrop that briefly surfaced off Sicily in 1831 before sinking back under the Mediterranean, claimed and contested by multiple nations in the few months it existed above water. It's a perfect Cogitore subject, a place that is simultaneously historical fact and geological rumor, and the works on view (grouped under titles like Incertitudes, Vigilances, Cendres and Prémonitions) treat that instability as their organizing logic.

Cogitore, better known to many for his film and video work exploring ritual, belief and contested territory, brings the same interests to these object-based pieces: a fascination with thresholds, half-documented events, and the way collective anxiety attaches itself to unstable ground. The show follows presentations of the same body of work at Madre in Naples and Mucem in Marseille, arriving in Paris as the exhibition's title suggests: an island that keeps reappearing under different institutional skies.

It's a tightly focused solo debut rather than a survey, built around a single mythic hook, and it rewards viewers willing to sit with ambiguity: nothing here resolves into a clean historical account, and that unresolve is the point.

shows.title: Summer Sun: Open my Heart
shows.description:
Robert Kushner has spent decades folding botanical imagery into paintings that refuse to sit quietly within either abstraction or decoration, and this new solo show brings together twelve works made between 2019 and 2025, most on Japanese paper, one on canvas, all built around flowers rendered with a gilded, pattern-heavy exuberance. Chrysanthemums, sunflowers, asters and celosia appear less as botanical illustration than as vehicles for pure visual pleasure: saturated color, metallic ground, and a compositional looseness that owes as much to textile and screen painting traditions as to still life.

Kushner emerged from the Pattern and Decoration movement of the 1970s, and this body of work reads as a mature, confident continuation of that project's core argument, that pattern and ornament are legitimate, serious painting subjects rather than a lesser, merely decorative mode. The Japanese paper support matters here too, its absorbency and texture pulling the pigment into soft, bloom-like edges that a canvas wouldn't produce.

It's a warm, generous show, unapologetically about beauty and abundance, arriving as flowers in late summer and early autumn: chrysanthemums and asters that mark the turn of the season, painted with the same gilded intensity Kushner brings to everything he touches.

shows.title: Mémoires
shows.description:
Sergey Kononov paints quiet, close-cropped scenes of solitude and intimacy, faces and figures rendered in grainy, ochre-warm light that deliberately evokes the texture of old film stock. Mémoires (memories) gathers a new body of work from the Odesa-born, Paris-based painter, who trained at the École des Beaux-Arts de Paris and has spent the past decade refining a soft-focus realist style that sits somewhere between icon painting and Balthus.

The paintings work by withholding as much as they show: subjects are often caught mid-gesture, eyes closed or turned away, hair falling across faces, so that the emotional charge comes from atmosphere and light rather than legible narrative or expression. Kononov has spoken about wanting to recreate the grain and warmth of old film in paint, and that nostalgic, slightly hazy quality gives even contemporary subjects a sense of half-remembered distance, appropriate for a show explicitly framed around memory.

It's an intimate, unhurried body of work, more invested in mood and tenderness than incident, and it continues a run of gallery and institutional recognition for an artist whose paintings favor quiet accumulation of feeling over drama.

shows.title: la soustraite
shows.description:
Gyan Panchal works with objects he pulls out of recycling centers and reuse depots — pieces of plastic, foam, fabric, wood, "cooked by the sun" as the gallery text puts it — and reworks them through a slow, deliberate sequence of washing, cutting, wearing down, repainting and recombining. Nothing is polished into something new; the sculptures keep the traces of what they used to be while shifting into something closer to abstraction. la soustraite (roughly, "the one subtracted" or "the removed") names that process of withdrawal as a method: taking things apart and away rather than adding to them.

The exhibition follows Panchal's recent run of solo shows in France (Angle centre d'art contemporain, Treignac Project, Alea–Artagon) and his 2019 survey at the MAMC+ in Saint-Étienne, and continues the vocabulary he's built over two decades — object, threshold, and a kind of contemporary asceticism that resists the speed of consumption and extraction. It's a quiet, materially exacting show, more about sustained looking than spectacle, and rewards slowing down in front of single objects rather than moving quickly through the space.

Panchal's work sits in major French public collections (Musée d'Art Moderne de la Ville de Paris, Centre Pompidou, several FRACs) as well as at Lafayette Anticipations, and this is his return to Marcelle Alix, the gallery that has represented him for years.

shows.title: Travessia
shows.description:
Patricia Leite paints skies, horizons and half-remembered fragments of landscape — a dawn, a silhouetted branch, an abandoned lounge chair — built up in thin, glowing layers of diluted oil paint that give even her plainest compositions a strange inner light. Travessia (Crossing) brings new paintings made this year, including Minguante (Waning), Travessia II and a view of Paris itself, Nuvem rosa de Paris (The Pink Cloud of Paris), alongside a painting of the Chapel of the Rosary in Vence.

Leite trained through Brazil's early-1980s return-to-painting movement, absorbed and then set aside influences from Klee to Barnett Newman, and spent years developing a personal language centered on color as an emotional signal rather than description — moons, birds and stars appear at the edges of her compositions rather than the center, and the horizon line does most of the structural work. It's an unusually lyrical, unhurried kind of painting, closer to memory than observation, and this is a good showcase for a Brazilian painter whose work is still not widely seen in Paris.

The show opens on the gallery's Place des Vosges location, a fitting setting given the essay accompanying the show explicitly connects Leite's suspended, involuntary-memory way of seeing to Proust.

shows.title: Vie des Formes
shows.description:
Timed to Paris Design Week and AlUla's cultural season in Paris, Vie des Formes puts furniture, sculpture, video and hybrid objects from AlUla's design-residency program in dialogue with works from the Fondation's own collection (Fonds de dotation Famille Moulin). The premise is a blurred line between art and design: some pieces rework craft and vernacular forms, others use natural or recycled materials, and others borrow and subvert the look of industrial production.

The participant list is wide-ranging — Meriem Bennani, Katinka Bock, Camille Blatrix, Matthew Angelo Harrison, Lydia Ourahmane and Mathieu Mercier are shown alongside AlUla-affiliated designers and studios like Altin Studio, bahraini—danish, and Studio ThusThat — which makes for a show about circulation and hybridity as much as about any single medium. Expect an installation that's meant to be handled and lived with rather than viewed at a distance, backed by a week of talks, a solar-powered sound performance, and family workshops.

It's a short run — five days, tied tightly to the design-week calendar — so it functions more as an event-exhibition than a conventional gallery hang, and is worth planning around if you're interested in where contemporary art and design collecting overlap.

shows.title: Aux origines de l'abstraction, 1962-1968
shows.description:
This is an origin story told backwards. Kim Guiline (1936–2021) spent the decades after the mid-1970s refining a signature language of near-monochrome canvases — black, white, or a single primary color, animated only by repetitive raised brushstrokes and a cruciform void running through the surface. This show skips past that mature, tightly theorized body of work to look at what came before it: the formative decade between 1962 and 1968, when the Korean-born, Paris-trained painter was still working his way toward that reduction.

The paintings on view trace a fast unraveling of representation. Early landscapes with heavy impasto give way, by 1963, to flattened, schematic panoramas indebted to late Braque; by 1967 the referents disappear altogether, replaced by bold juxtaposed color planes, geometric bands, and hard-edged compositions that flirt with both Poliakoff's lyricism and the American hard-edge and minimalist painting Guiline encountered in Paris in the late 1960s.

It's a rarely-seen chapter — curated with the input of Musée Cernuschi's Maël Bellec — that reframes Guiline's later, more austere paintings not as a sudden signature style but as the endpoint of a genuine period of searching, essential to understanding how he arrived at the reductive vocabulary for which he's now best known.

shows.title: Carnets ouverts
shows.description:
Joanne Boyer's paintings are built out of light and shadow — figures, landscapes, and architecture emerging from pools of darkness in a way that owes an obvious debt to Caravaggio and Goya. Carnets ouverts (Open Notebooks) steps away from those finished paintings to show the works on paper underneath: gouaches and drawings, small in scale, more exposed in gesture.

Born in 1990 in Versailles, Boyer draws from a personal bestiary of ruined landscapes, forests, sirens, satyrs, and knights, mixed in with unmistakably contemporary details — a coexistence of timelines she doesn't try to resolve into a single narrative. On paper, that vocabulary becomes looser and more immediate: motifs get tried, repeated, abandoned, and picked up again, less as sketches for future paintings than as an autonomous, ongoing record of how her images form.

Shown together for the first time, these sheets offer an unusually intimate way into Boyer's practice — not the polished result but the circulation of ideas that feeds it.

shows.title: La Dolce Vista
shows.description:
Claude Nori has spent half a century photographing summer as a state of mind as much as a season — sunlit bodies on Italian and French beaches, teenagers loitering in the heat, the loose, affectionate intimacy of the Mediterranean everyday. A key figure of the "Photographie Subjective" movement he helped found in the 1970s, Nori works in a warm, unposed, snapshot-adjacent register that treats color and light as emotional material rather than just documentary fact.

La Dolce Vista, opening with the artist present, promises more of that sensibility: a title that puns on la dolce vita while keeping the photographer's gaze — vista — front and center. Expect the loose-limbed, nostalgic romanticism that has made Nori a reference point for a generation of younger photographers working in saturated color.
shows.reception: Thursday, September 10, 6pm-8:30pm, in the presence of the artist

shows.title: Attending
shows.description: Lee Bae's ninth solo show with Perrotin Paris follows a year of museum surveys in Wonju, Shunde and the Abbaye de Beaulieu-en-Rouergue. The Korean artist works almost entirely in charcoal: burned pine bound into large sculptures, ground into ink for the sweeping black Brushstroke paintings, and pressed into surfaces that read as both ash and growth. Attending adds new large-scale sculptures, an in-situ installation built for the Turenne galleries and a performance video, all circling his idea of charcoal as fire's afterlife: matter that has been destroyed and holds the energy to begin again.

shows.title: Alma Allen
shows.description: The self-taught American sculptor Alma Allen debuts with Perrotin in its Impasse Saint-Claude space. Allen carves wood and stone and casts bronze, often from material found near his studio in Tepoztlán, Mexico, into forms that look like roots, seed pods, shells and fossils. Each piece starts as string, clay or wax worked through his fingers until it finds its balance, and the finished sculptures keep that hand-held intimacy even at monumental scale. They feel talismanic and slightly uncanny, familiar shapes from the natural world that refuse to settle into a category.

shows.title: Winter Sun
shows.description: Jordan Casteel's first exhibition in France, and the biggest showing of her work in Europe so far, fills Ropac's Marais gallery with paintings made in the first half of 2026. Casteel is known for large, warm portraits of people from her own community in Harlem and upstate New York; here the palette cools to the earthy greys, blues and browns of deep winter light. Portraits sit alongside landscapes and botanical close-ups, and the show reads as a meditation on dormancy and renewal, grief and love, with the people and places around her as anchors.

shows.title: The Venice Paintings
shows.description: After showing them at the Palazzo Cini during this year's Venice Biennale, David Salle brings the same group of paintings to an intimate room at Ropac's Pantin site. Salle trained an AI model on his own Tapestry Paintings of 1989–91, themselves based on 18th-century Russian tapestries that copied Italian oil paintings, and then painted the results by hand. The canvases collapse four centuries of copying into one dense, layered surface, and Salle presents the collaboration less as surrender to the machine than as a way of bending it back toward painting.

shows.title: Works from the 1960s
shows.description: The first solo presentation of Lee Krasner in France, at Gagosian's rue de Ponthieu gallery, zooms in on the decade when she came fully into her own after Jackson Pollock's death. The paintings are big and fast: the ecstatic color of Icarus and Comet, and the long horizontal Portrait in Green of 1969, alongside gouache collages on paper. The show coincides with the Met's Krasner and Pollock exhibition in New York and makes a strong case for Krasner as one of the most inventive painters of her generation rather than a footnote to her husband.

shows.title: Rudolf Stingel
shows.description: A single new painting fills Gagosian's rue de Castiglione gallery: Rudolf Stingel's monumental view of the New York skyline, more than four meters wide, rendered in oil and enamel from a photograph with his usual uncanny fidelity. Stingel has spent recent years painting self-portraits and Alpine scenes from snapshots; here he turns the camera outward. Like Morandi's bottles or Canaletto's canals, the familiar subject becomes a study in looking, and up close the photographic surface dissolves into brushwork, smudges and the traces of the hand.

shows.title: Unfinished thinking: Paintings and Social Maps
shows.description: Oscar Murillo fills Zwirner's Marais gallery with new paintings and the latest of his Social Maps, collective works built from the marks of strangers. For years Murillo has sent blank canvases to schools around the world and asked students to draw on them; their doodles, words and scribbles become the ground of large, layered surfaces that he then works into. The paintings in this show are dense and frenetic, full of scraped color and fragments of text, and they carry the energy of many hands and places, from Colombia and Cameroon to the Philippines and Poland.

shows.title: Tacita Dean and Bruce Nauman
shows.description: Two artists who rarely collaborate share Marian Goodman's Paris gallery with Drawing Blind Drawing, a new 35mm film diptych. Dean and Nauman met in early 2025 and talked about drawing: Nauman had just returned to it after nearly twenty years, working in gold- and silverpoint and filming himself drawing blind, from memory, with a 3D iPhone rig of his own making. Dean, a lifelong champion of photochemical film, brought her camera. The result is a quiet, absorbing portrait of two hands at work, and of two very different artists finding common ground in the oldest of mediums.

shows.title: ŒuVreS réCEnteS
shows.description: Jutta Koether's first solo show at Chantal Crousel marks a return to Paris, where she lived briefly in the early 1990s. The German painter, musician and critic has long built her work out of other people's paintings, reworking Cézanne, Twombly, Auerbach and Giacometti not as homage but as a way of putting images into conversation. This new group of canvases revisits some of the artistic and literary references that shaped her, in her signature hot palette and agitated, layered brushwork, with the cheeky typography of the title setting the tone.

shows.title: In This Time
shows.description: For his second show with Chantal Crousel, on the second floor of 10 rue Charlot, Nick Mauss scales up his reverse paintings on mirrored glass to the height of the viewer. Folded around closed volumes, the panels catch slanting reflections of the room and of the people moving through it, so the paintings keep changing as you walk around them. Mauss has spent two decades refusing hierarchies between painting, drawing, writing, performance and display, and these pieces fold all of that into objects that are part painting, part furniture and part stage set.

shows.title: Selection of works
shows.artist: Tarek Atoui, Roberto Cuoghi, Pierre Huyghe, Amy Sillman, Haegue Yang
shows.description: A short group presentation centred on Tarek Atoui's At-Tāriq, three sculptures from an ongoing series inspired by the majlis, the room for hospitality and gathering in Arab and North African homes. Atoui built the project from years of research along the trans-Saharan pilgrimage and trade routes, combining traditional musical instruments, craft techniques and contemporary sound, and the pieces work as both sculptures and instruments. They are shown with recent works by Roberto Cuoghi, Pierre Huyghe, Amy Sillman and Haegue Yang. The last days are this week.

shows.title: Les Fous d'En Face
shows.description: Elmgreen & Dragset take over both of Max Hetzler's Paris spaces, facing each other at 46 and 57 rue du Temple, for their first show there. The title means The Fools on the Other Side, and the duo stage three new installations across the street that play with their trademark absurd humour, displaced interiors and open-ended stories. Part of the show looks back at their own history together, and as always the joke lands a little uneasily: familiar rooms and objects turn strange when moved just slightly out of place.

shows.title: I will miss you Yesterday I will miss you Today I will miss you Tomorrow And that's how it will Always be
shows.description: Tracey Emin's first solo show at White Cube's Paris gallery, an apartment-like space on avenue Matignon, plays to its domestic scale. New paintings and small bronzes unfold as a run of intimate scenes charting love through closeness and estrangement, almost all set in the bedroom. Emin's loose, urgent brushwork renders a nude woman sometimes held by a lover but more often alone, drifting in fields of night blue and black. It is unguarded, autobiographical work from an artist who has made painting her main language in recent years.

shows.title: Calder: François Premier
shows.description: In 1953 Alexander Calder moved back to France after twenty years away, first near Aix-en-Provence and then to Saché in the Loire Valley, where he worked in a 17th-century stone house called François Premier. Hauser & Wirth's Paris gallery, by happy coincidence an hôtel particulier on rue François 1er, now devotes the first major show to that postwar chapter. Mobiles, stabiles and the ink-and-gouache paintings he made in the Provençal landscape show how freely Calder worked once settled in France, a period that ended with his triumphant return to the Paris galleries in 1954.

shows.title: Kind of Blue
shows.description: Arlene Shechet's first exhibition with Galerie Lelong brings recent sculptures by the New York artist who did more than anyone in the last twenty years to bring ceramics back into the center of contemporary sculpture. Shechet's pieces lurch, slump and balance in ways clay is not supposed to, glazed in deep blues, pinks and metallic skins and often perched on cast or carved bases that become part of the work. Celebrated in the US since her mid-career retrospective, she is less known in France, and this tight selection is a good introduction to her improvised, funny and bodily forms.

shows.title: Théâtre imaginaire
shows.description: Galerie Lelong introduces Magnus Plessen with about twenty paintings from 2024 to 2026 in its avenue Matignon space. Born in Hamburg in 1967 and self-taught, Plessen came to painting by way of photography and film and has painted full time since 1999. His canvases build bodies, faces, flowers and studio interiors out of fragments, with figures assembled from flat planes of color and parts left blank, as if images were being pieced together from memory. The title suggests a stage, and the paintings feel like scenes caught midway between appearing and dissolving.

shows.title: Estampes choisies
shows.artist: Mamma Andersson, Nalini Malani, Alison Saar
shows.description: A three-woman print show in Lelong's rue de Téhéran space pairs the Swedish painter Mamma Andersson, the Indian artist Nalini Malani and the American sculptor Alison Saar. They come from three continents and work in very different styles, but each has a strong graphic hand and a fascination with storytelling, myth and the body. Andersson's hushed, melancholy interiors and landscapes sit beside Malani's fierce mythological figures and Saar's woodcut-like images of Black women, and the prints make a compact, affordable way into three major careers.

shows.title: Érotique
shows.description: About forty wood sculptures from 1988 to 2026 by Wang Keping, a founder of the dissident Stars Group in Beijing who has lived in France since 1984, fill Nathalie Obadia's gallery on rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré. After recent outings at the Musée Guimet, the Musée Rodin gardens, Chambord and Fontainebleau, this show narrows in on the erotic side of his work. Carved from single logs that keep their knots and grain, his rounded couples, heads and torsos are sensual and abstracted, and the wood's natural shapes seem to suggest the embrace rather than the other way around.

shows.title: Avant et après l'Arte Povera
shows.description: Galleria Continua's Marais space looks at Michelangelo Pistoletto on either side of Arte Povera, the Italian movement he helped found in the 1960s. Pistoletto made his name with the mirror paintings, figures printed on polished steel that pull viewers and the room into the picture, and went on to the rag-and-statue Venus and decades of participatory projects. The show traces how the questions he asked before 1967, about the image, the spectator and time, carried through everything he made after, with the mirror as the thread.

shows.title: Afterimage
shows.description: Hank Willis Thomas fills Continua's Faubourg Saint-Honoré space with his retroreflective works, which look like faint, almost blank images in ambient light and flash into full photographs when lit from the viewer's position, for instance by a phone flash. Thomas builds them from press and archival images of protest, sport and Black American history, so that seeing the picture literally depends on how you look. The gallery shows them both ways, and the experience of a hidden image coming forward is the point: history that is there all along but only appears when you choose to illuminate it.

shows.title: Philippe Parreno
shows.description: Esther Schipper turns its apartment-like gallery on Place Vendôme into a domestic interior that Philippe Parreno sets in slow motion. At its center is Membrane, a cluster of antennae that senses temperature, pressure, humidity and even breath, and uses the data to drive light and movement through the rooms. Two motorized blinds open and close independently across the windows like eyelids, changing the light on everything inside. Nothing happens the same way twice, and the show is less a set of objects than a choreography of weather, architecture and time.
